title: How to start doing more volume in your training
summary: NH explains why jumping from novice 3x5/5x5 programs to pre-made high-volume programs like 10x10 fails. Volume must be built slowly from your current workload while staying in relevant intensity windows, ideally via evolving rep ranges within a 2-15 rep zone.
claims: The advice to do more volume for hypertrophy is accurate; the problem is a drastic spike in volume when the body isn't prepared
People who jump volume too fast get no results, can't recover or get injured, then wrongly blame volume itself
A 5x5 on one lift is manageable, but 5x5 spread across variations and accessories throughout a program quickly adds up to a different beast
There should be a middle ground between novice and high-volume programs: a bridge program, or novice programs that push volume a bit more; novices are not made of sugar
Many volume programs over-tax certain body parts, ignore mechanical failure and tendon pain and neglect recovery
Volume cannot exist without intensity and frequency; sets done outside relevant intensity windows are junk volume
3-4 sets of 30 reps or 10x10 on squats are extreme and not beneficial
Programs that advertise high intensity tend to lack volume and high-volume programs tend to lack intensity; be wary of both
Take the tonnage you did as a novice and build up slowly: add a rep here, lower the weight, add one back-off set at the end for squats or bench
Building the work capacity to train two hours with heavy loads might take 3-4 years, and the adaptation itself is training stimulus
Most people training for bodybuilding should stay between 2 and 15 reps; singles aren't best for hypertrophy and above 15 you enter junk volume
Within the 2-15 window each person can lean higher or lower reps, and preferences can differ lift to lift
To start doing more volume, turn a rep range you like, such as 3x5, into an evolving rep range
